claim: Fed flies show taste aversion to acetic acid.
source: Fed flies show taste aversion to acetic acid, whereas starved flies show a robust appetitive response.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing that fed flies do not exhibit PER to acetic acid alone and that acetic acid suppresses sucrose-evoked PER in fed flies.

claim: Starved flies show a robust appetitive response to acetic acid.
source: Fed flies show taste aversion to acetic acid, whereas starved flies show a robust appetitive response.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing that starved flies exhibit strong PER to acetic acid.

claim: The opposing responses to acetic acid are mediated by two different classes of taste neurons, the sugar- and bitter-sensing neurons.
source: These opposing responses are mediated by two different classes of taste neurons, the sugar- and bitter-sensing neurons.
evidence: Supported by genetic silencing experiments and calcium imaging data.

claim: Hunger shifts the behavioral response from aversion to attraction by enhancing the appetitive sugar pathway as well as suppressing the aversive bitter pathway.
source: Hunger shifts the behavioral response from aversion to attraction by enhancing the appetitive sugar pathway as well as suppressing the aversive bitter pathway.
evidence: Supported by genetic silencing experiments showing differential effects of hunger on sugar and bitter pathways.

claim: A single tastant can drive opposing behaviors by activating distinct taste pathways modulated by internal state.
source: Thus a single tastant can drive opposing behaviors by activating distinct taste pathways modulated by internal state.
evidence: Supported by behavioral and imaging data showing acetic acid activates both sugar and bitter neurons with state-dependent behavioral outcomes.

claim: During fermentation, yeast and bacteria enzymatically convert six-carbon sugars into ethanol and acetic acid.
source: During fermentation, yeast and bacteria enzymatically convert six-carbon sugars into ethanol and acetic acid.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about fermentation processes.

claim: The scent of decaying fruit is attractive to Drosophila melanogaster.
source: These fermentation products can be toxic to the fly, yet the scent of decaying fruit is attractive and moreover the fly feeds despite the presence of these toxic compounds (McKenzie and Parsons, 1972; McKenzie and McKechnie, 1979; Zhu et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster feeds on decaying fruit despite the presence of toxic compounds.
source: These fermentation products can be toxic to the fly, yet the scent of decaying fruit is attractive and moreover the fly feeds despite the presence of these toxic compounds (McKenzie and Parsons, 1972; McKenzie and McKechnie, 1979; Zhu et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cider vinegar elicits strong odor-evoked attraction in Drosophila.
source: Cider vinegar, for example, contains the potentially toxic metabolite acetic acid but elicits strong odor-evoked attraction (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster is more resistant to the toxic effects of acetic acid than other Drosophila species that do not depend upon fermenting food sources.
source: Drosophila melanogaster, termed the vinegar fly, is more resistant to the toxic effects of acetic acid than other Drosophila species that do not depend upon fermenting food sources and shows greater tolerance to acetic acid than structurally similar carboxylic acids (McKenzie and McKechnie, 1979; Parsons, 1980; Chakir et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster shows greater tolerance to acetic acid than structurally similar carboxylic acids.
source: Drosophila melanogaster, termed the vinegar fly, is more resistant to the toxic effects of acetic acid than other Drosophila species that do not depend upon fermenting food sources and shows greater tolerance to acetic acid than structurally similar carboxylic acids (McKenzie and McKechnie, 1979; Parsons, 1980; Chakir et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Flies can utilize acetic acid as a caloric source when deprived of other food sources.
source: Moreover, flies can utilize acetic acid as a caloric source when deprived of other food sources (Parsons, 1980; Hoffmann and Parsons, 1984); acetic acid is converted into acetyl-CoA and metabolized by the tricarboxylic acid cycle.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Acetic acid is converted into acetyl-CoA and metabolized by the tricarboxylic acid cycle.
source: Moreover, flies can utilize acetic acid as a caloric source when deprived of other food sources (Parsons, 1980; Hoffmann and Parsons, 1984); acetic acid is converted into acetyl-CoA and metabolized by the tricarboxylic acid cycle.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Feeding is initiated by extension of the proboscis, a behavior that allows the fly to taste a potential food source.
source: Feeding is initiated by extension of the proboscis, a behavior that allows the fly to taste a potential food source (Dethier, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Flies recognize a relatively small number of basic taste categories, including sweet, salty, bitter, sour, fat, and carbonation.
source: Flies recognize a relatively small number of basic taste categories, including sweet, salty, bitter, sour, fat, and carbonation (Liman et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2013; Jaeger et al., 2018; Chen and Amrein, 2017; Masek and Keene, 2013; Fischler et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most tastants excite only one class of sensory neurons in flies.
source: As in mammals, most tastants excite only one class of sensory neurons and each class is thought to activate determined neural pathways to elicit innate behavioral responses (Liman et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Activation of sugar-responsive neurons drives appetitive feeding responses.
source: For example, activation of sugar-responsive neurons drives appetitive feeding responses, whereas bitter-responsive neurons elicit aversion and suppress feeding (Liman et al., 2014; Marella et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bitter-responsive neurons elicit aversion and suppress feeding.
source: For example, activation of sugar-responsive neurons drives appetitive feeding responses, whereas bitter-responsive neurons elicit aversion and suppress feeding (Liman et al., 2014; Marella et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both flies and mammals generally exhibit taste aversion to strongly acidic food.
source: Both flies and mammals generally exhibit taste aversion to strongly acidic food (Charlu et al., 2013; DeSimone et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Flies show greater sugar consumption at an acidic pH than at a neutral or basic pH.
source: However, flies do not uniformly avoid acidic stimuli: they show greater sugar consumption at an acidic pH than at a neutral or basic pH (Deshpande et al., 2015), and at low concentration acids may counteract the repulsive effect of bitter compounds on feeding (Chen and Amrein, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: At low concentration acids may counteract the repulsive effect of bitter compounds on feeding.
source: However, flies do not uniformly avoid acidic stimuli: they show greater sugar consumption at an acidic pH than at a neutral or basic pH (Deshpande et al., 2015), and at low concentration acids may counteract the repulsive effect of bitter compounds on feeding (Chen and Amrein, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Flies prefer to lay eggs on carboxylic acids such as acetic and citric acid.
source: Flies also prefer to lay eggs on carboxylic acids such as acetic and citric acid (Joseph et al., 2009; Chen and Amrein, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ovipositional preference for acids is mediated by taste sensory neurons in the legs that respond specifically to acids.
source: This ovipositional preference is mediated by taste sensory neurons in the legs that respond specifically to acids (Chen and Amrein, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Dedicated acid-sensing neurons in the proboscis have not been identified.
source: Dedicated acid-sensing neurons in the proboscis have not been identified, although acid responses in bitter-sensing neurons have been observed (Charlu et al., 2013; Rimal et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acid responses in bitter-sensing neurons have been observed.
source: Dedicated acid-sensing neurons in the proboscis have not been identified, although acid responses in bitter-sensing neurons have been observed (Charlu et al., 2013; Rimal et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hunger elicits several adaptive changes in behavior: increased food-seeking and food consumption, enhanced locomotor activity, decreased sleep, and altered olfactory and taste sensitivity.
source: Hunger elicits several adaptive changes in behavior: increased food-seeking and food consumption, enhanced locomotor activity, decreased sleep, and altered olfactory and taste sensitivity (Sternson et al., 2013; Itskov and Ribeiro, 2013; Pool and Scott, 2014; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In flies, starvation increases sugar sensitivity, which promotes feeding.
source: In flies, starvation increases sugar sensitivity, which promotes feeding, and decreases bitter sensitivity, which enhances acceptance of food sources that contain aversive tastants (Inagaki et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Starvation decreases bitter sensitivity, which enhances acceptance of food sources that contain aversive tastants.
source: In flies, starvation increases sugar sensitivity, which promotes feeding, and decreases bitter sensitivity, which enhances acceptance of food sources that contain aversive tastants (Inagaki et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Starved flies show enhanced olfactory attraction to cider vinegar, which facilitates food search behavior.
source: Starved flies also show enhanced olfactory attraction to cider vinegar, which facilitates food search behavior (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Hunger-dependent changes in both olfactory and gustatory sensitivity result, at least in part, from alterations in sensory neuron activity.
source: These hunger-dependent changes in both olfactory and gustatory sensitivity result, at least in part, from alterations in sensory neuron activity (Inagaki et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014; Root et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Flies avoid residing on food containing acetic acid.
source: Acetic acid, however, can be toxic and flies avoid residing on food containing acetic acid (Parsons, 1980; Joseph et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In fed flies, exposure of acetic acid (1–10%) to the labellum elicited very weak levels of PER similar to those induced by water.
source: In fed flies, exposure of acetic acid (1–10%) to the labellum elicited very weak levels of PER similar to those induced by water (Figure 1A), even though these flies showed strong PER to sucrose (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fed flies showed strong PER to sucrose.
source: In fed flies, exposure of acetic acid (1–10%) to the labellum elicited very weak levels of PER similar to those induced by water (Figure 1A), even though these flies showed strong PER to sucrose (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: When acetic acid was mixed with either 300 mM or 50 mM sucrose it strongly reduced sucrose-evoked PER in fed flies.
source: Moreover, when acetic acid was mixed with either 300 mM or 50 mM sucrose it strongly reduced sucrose-evoked PER in fed flies (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: 79% of fed flies exhibited PER to 300 mM sucrose alone, and this response was reduced to 44% when 10% acetic acid was added.
source: 79% of fed flies exhibited PER to 300 mM sucrose alone, and this response was reduced to 44% when 10% acetic acid was added (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When acetic acid was applied to the labellum of one- or two-day starved flies, strong, dose-dependent PER was observed.
source: When acetic acid was applied to the labellum of one- or two-day starved flies, strong, dose-dependent PER was observed, with 86% of flies exhibiting PER to 10% acetic acid after two days of starvation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 86% of flies exhibited PER to 10% acetic acid after two days of starvation.
source: When acetic acid was applied to the labellum of one- or two-day starved flies, strong, dose-dependent PER was observed, with 86% of flies exhibiting PER to 10% acetic acid after two days of starvation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When acetic acid was added to concentrations of sucrose ranging from 5 mM to 300 mM, no suppression of sugar-evoked PER was observed in two-day starved flies.
source: Moreover, when acetic acid was added to concentrations of sucrose ranging from 5 mM to 300 mM, no suppression of sugar-evoked PER was observed in two-day starved flies; in fact, the addition of acetic acid enhanced PER to 5 or 10 mM sucrose (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of acetic acid enhanced PER to 5 or 10 mM sucrose in two-day starved flies.
source: Moreover, when acetic acid was added to concentrations of sucrose ranging from 5 mM to 300 mM, no suppression of sugar-evoked PER was observed in two-day starved flies; in fact, the addition of acetic acid enhanced PER to 5 or 10 mM sucrose (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In one-day starved flies, acetic acid weakly suppressed PER at 50 mM but not 300 mM sucrose.
source: In one-day starved flies, acetic acid weakly suppressed PER at 50 mM but not 300 mM sucrose (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The switch from an aversive response in fed flies to an appetitive response in starved flies is specific for acetic acid and was not observed for other aversive tastants, such as the bitter compounds quinine and lobeline.
source: This switch from an aversive response in fed flies to an appetitive response in starved flies is specific for acetic acid and was not observed for other aversive tastants, such as the bitter compounds quinine and lobeline (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Appetitive compounds such as sugar do not elicit a qualitative switch in behavior, since sugar elicited PER in both fed and starved flies.
source: Appetitive compounds such as sugar also do not elicit a qualitative switch in behavior, since sugar elicited PER in both fed and starved flies (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Acetic acid elicits strong PER in starved flies when applied to the legs.
source: We first confirmed that acetic acid elicits strong PER in starved flies when applied to the legs instead of the labellum (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In 72% of trials, starved flies that showed PER extended the proboscis in the direction of the stimulus when legs were stimulated asymmetrically with acetic acid.
source: We then stimulated the legs asymmetrically and observed that in 72% of trials, starved flies that showed PER extended the proboscis in the direction of the stimulus (Figure 1F, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Video 1.

claim: Proboscis extension was never observed in the direction opposing the stimulus.
source: Proboscis extension was never observed in the direction opposing the stimulus, and in 28% of trials flies exhibited PER neither toward nor away from the stimulus (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: When afforded the option to consume 5% acetic acid following PER, 7 of the 10 flies tested consumed it.
source: When afforded the option to consume 5% acetic acid following PER, 7 of the 10 flies tested consumed it (Video 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Video 2.

claim: Starved flies failed to show PER to hydrochloric acid at pH values equivalent to those of 5% or 10% acetic acid.
source: Starved flies failed to show PER to hydrochloric acid at pH values equivalent to those of 5% or 10% acetic acid, which elicit strong PER, indicating that low pH is not sufficient to induce an appetitive response (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Low pH is not sufficient to induce an appetitive response in starved flies.
source: Starved flies failed to show PER to hydrochloric acid at pH values equivalent to those of 5% or 10% acetic acid, which elicit strong PER, indicating that low pH is not sufficient to induce an appetitive response (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Starved flies failed to observe a response to potassium acetate at molarities equivalent to those of 5% or 10% acetic acid.
source: We also tested the response of starved flies to potassium acetate at molarities equivalent to those of 5% or 10% acetic acid and failed to observe a response (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Neither protons nor acetate ions are capable of eliciting PER.
source: These experiments suggest that neither protons nor acetate ions are capable of eliciting PER, suggesting that undissociated acetic acid is recognized by taste cells.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing no PER to HCl or potassium acetate.

claim: Undissociated acetic acid is recognized by taste cells.
source: These experiments suggest that neither protons nor acetate ions are capable of eliciting PER, suggesting that undissociated acetic acid is recognized by taste cells.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing no PER to HCl or potassium acetate.

claim: Propionic acid, a simple carboxylic acid structurally similar to acetic acid, elicited strong PER in starved flies.
source: In accord with this suggestion, propionic acid, a simple carboxylic acid structurally similar to acetic acid, elicited strong PER in starved flies whereas the more distantly related citric acid elicited a weaker response (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Citric acid elicited a weaker response than propionic acid in starved flies.
source: In accord with this suggestion, propionic acid, a simple carboxylic acid structurally similar to acetic acid, elicited strong PER in starved flies whereas the more distantly related citric acid elicited a weaker response (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Undissociated small aliphatic acids may be recognized by gustatory neurons to elicit PER in starved flies.
source: Thus, undissociated small aliphatic acids may be recognized by gustatory neurons to elicit PER in starved flies.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing PER to propionic acid but not to HCl or potassium acetate.

claim: Acetic acid activates olfactory sensory neurons.
source: Acetic acid activates olfactory sensory neurons (Ai et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PER to acetic acid was unperturbed by removal of olfactory organs in two-day starved flies.
source: We therefore removed the olfactory organs, the third antennal segment and maxillary palp, from two-day starved flies and observed that PER to acetic acid was unperturbed by this manipulation (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 76% of flies lacking olfactory organs showed PER to 10% acetic acid, a value close to that observed with control flies (72%).
source: 76% of flies lacking olfactory organs showed PER to 10% acetic acid, a value close to that observed with control flies (72%; Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fed flies lacking olfactory organs failed to show PER to acetic acid, mirroring the behavior of control flies.
source: Fed flies lacking olfactory organs failed to show PER to acetic acid, mirroring the behavior of control flies (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Fed flies lacking olfactory organs showed aversion to acetic acid, as observed by significant suppression of PER when acetic acid was added to sucrose.
source: Fed flies lacking olfactory organs also continued to show aversion to acetic acid, as we observed significant suppression of PER when acetic acid was added to sucrose (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both the appetitive and aversive proboscis extension responses to acetic acid are observed in the absence of olfactory organs, and are likely to be mediated by the gustatory system.
source: These experiments demonstrate that both the appetitive and aversive proboscis extension responses to acetic acid are observed in the absence of olfactory organs, and are likely to be mediated by the gustatory system.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing PER to acetic acid in flies lacking olfactory organs.

claim: Starved poxn∆M22-B5 homozygous mutants failed to display PER to any concentration of acetic acid tested.
source: Starved poxn∆M22-B5 homozygous mutants failed to display PER to any concentration of acetic acid tested (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Wild-type flies, poxn∆M22-B5/+ heterozygotes, and rescue flies showed strong PER to acetic acid, with up to ~50–70% of flies responding.
source: In contrast, wild-type flies, poxn∆M22-B5/+heterozygotes (which have normal bristles), and rescue flies (poxn∆M22-B5 mutants carrying the SuperA rescue transgene; Boll and Noll, 2002) showed strong PER, with up to ~50–70% of flies responding (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The appetitive and aversive responses to acetic acid require the taste organs and are largely independent of olfaction.
source: Nonetheless, these experiments suggest that the appetitive and aversive responses to acetic acid require the taste organs and are largely independent of olfaction.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data with poxn mutants and flies lacking olfactory organs.

claim: Sugar-sensing neurons express multiple chemoreceptors and elicit PER in response to sugars.
source: Sugar-sensing neurons express multiple chemoreceptors and elicit PER in response to sugars (Dahanukar et al., 2007; Slone et al., 2007; Fujii et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The receptor Gr64f is expressed in all sugar-responsive taste neurons.
source: The receptor Gr64f is expressed in all sugar-responsive taste neurons (Fujii et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Starved flies harboring both the Gr64f-Gal4 and UAS-Kir2.1 transgenes showed very low frequencies of PER (12–28%) in response to increasing concentrations of either sucrose or acetic acid.
source: Starved flies harboring both the Gr64f-Gal4 and UAS-Kir2.1 transgenes showed very low frequencies of PER (12–28%) in response to increasing concentrations of either sucrose or acetic acid (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Control flies containing either the Gr64f-Gal4 or UAS-Kir2.1 transgenes alone exhibited strong PER to both sucrose and acetic acid, with 100% of flies responding to sucrose and ~70–80% responding to acetic acid.
source: Control flies containing either the Gr64f-Gal4 or UAS-Kir2.1 transgenes alone resembled wild-type flies and exhibited strong PER to both sucrose and acetic acid, with 100% of flies responding to sucrose and ~70–80% responding to acetic acid (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The appetitive response to acetic acid observed in starved flies is mediated by the sugar-sensing neurons.
source: These experiments demonstrate that the appetitive response to acetic acid observed in starved flies is mediated by the sugar-sensing neurons.
evidence: Inferred from genetic silencing experiments showing loss of PER to acetic acid when sugar neurons are silenced.

claim: Eight Grs are expressed in sugar sensory neurons of the labellum.
source: Eight Grs are expressed in sugar sensory neurons of the labellum (Fujii et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Homozygous flies carrying deletions in all eight sugar-sensing Gr genes (∆8Grs/∆8Grs) showed a strong reduction in PER to sucrose as compared with control heterozygous flies.
source: As expected, homozygous flies carrying deletions in all eight sugar-sensing Gr genes (∆8Grs/∆8Grs; Yavuz et al., 2014) showed a strong reduction in PER to sucrose as compared with control heterozygous flies (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Homozygous mutant flies lacking all eight sugar Grs continued to show PER to acetic acid.
source: In contrast to their strongly reduced response to sugar, homozygous mutant flies continued to show PER to acetic acid (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Acetic acid-evoked PER in homozygous mutant flies lacking all eight sugar Grs was significantly greater than in control flies.
source: Interestingly, acetic acid-evoked PER in homozygous mutant flies was significantly greater than in control flies (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The response to acetic acid in starved flies is mediated by the sugar-sensing neurons but does not employ the sugar receptors.
source: Overall, these experiments demonstrate that the response to acetic acid in starved flies is mediated by the sugar-sensing neurons but does not employ the sugar receptors.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing PER to acetic acid in flies lacking sugar receptors.

claim: The sugar-sensing neurons also elicit PER in response to fatty acids, such as hexanoic and octanoic acid, through a molecular mechanism distinct from sugar detection.
source: The sugar-sensing neurons also elicit PER in response to fatty acids, such as hexanoic and octanoic acid, through a molecular mechanism distinct from sugar detection (Masek and Keene, 2013; Tauber et al., 2017; Ahn et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PER induced by fatty acids requires phospholipase C (PLC) signaling in sugar-sensing neurons whereas PLC is dispensable for PER to sucrose.
source: A previous study showed that PER induced by fatty acids requires phospholipase C (PLC) signaling in sugar-sensing neurons whereas PLC is dispensable for PER to sucrose (Masek and Keene, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: RNAi inhibition of norpA expression in the sugar neurons severely reduced PER to fatty acids whereas PER to either sucrose or acetic acid was unaffected.
source: RNAi inhibition of norpA expression in the sugar neurons severely reduced PER to fatty acids whereas PER to either sucrose or acetic acid was unaffected (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: The appetitive response to acetic acid is mediated by sugar-sensing neurons, but engages molecular pathways distinct from those employed in the detection of either sugars or fatty acids.
source: These data suggest that the appetitive response to acetic acid is mediated by sugar-sensing neurons, but engages molecular pathways distinct from those employed in the detection of either sugars or fatty acids.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing PER to acetic acid is not affected by loss of sugar receptors or norpA.

claim: Multiple classes of bitter sensory neurons reside in the labellum, and each of these neurons expresses the receptor Gr66a.
source: Multiple classes of bitter sensory neurons reside in the labellum, and each of these neurons expresses the receptor Gr66a (Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Starved control flies exhibit PER to sucrose, and this response is strongly diminished by the addition of the bitter compounds quinine or lobeline.
source: Starved control flies exhibit PER to sucrose, and this response is strongly diminished by the addition of the bitter compounds quinine or lobeline (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Suppression of PER by bitter compounds is no longer observed when Kir2.1 is expressed in bitter neurons.
source: This suppression of PER by bitter compounds is no longer observed when Kir2.1 is expressed in bitter neurons, demonstrating the efficacy of Kir2.1 silencing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: In control fed flies acetic acid suppressed PER to sucrose, but this suppression was largely eliminated when the bitter neurons were silenced.
source: In control fed flies acetic acid suppressed PER to sucrose, but this suppression was largely eliminated when the bitter neurons were silenced (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In controls, ~80% of flies exhibited PER to sucrose alone, and this was reduced to ~20–30% upon addition of 10% acetic acid.
source: In controls,~80% of flies exhibited PER to sucrose alone, and this was reduced to ~20–30% upon addition of 10% acetic acid.
evidence: Supported by experimental data.

claim: When bitter neurons were silenced over 80% of flies continued to exhibit PER upon exposure to a mixture of sugar and 10% acetic acid.
source: In contrast, when bitter neurons were silenced over 80% of flies continued to exhibit PER upon exposure to a mixture of sugar and 10% acetic acid (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Bitter-sensing neurons mediate the aversive response to acetic acid in fed flies.
source: These results indicate that bitter-sensing neurons mediate the aversive response to acetic acid in fed flies.
evidence: Inferred from genetic silencing experiments showing loss of aversion when bitter neurons are silenced.

claim: Acetic acid elicited PER in ~20% of control fed flies, a value near baseline.
source: Acetic acid elicited PER in ~20% of control fed flies, a value near baseline (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Silencing of the bitter neurons resulted in a striking increase in the percentage of fed flies that exhibited PER to acetic acid (~60–80%).
source: Silencing of the bitter neurons resulted in a striking increase in the percentage of fed flies that exhibited PER to acetic acid (~60–80%; Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Silencing bitter neurons in fed flies did not affect PER to sucrose alone.
source: Silencing bitter neurons in fed flies did not affect PER to sucrose alone, indicating that the bitter neurons do not exert nonspecific suppression of PER (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Fed flies normally fail to exhibit PER to acetic acid because acetic acid activates sugar-sensing neurons, which promote an appetitive response, but in the fed state simultaneous activation of bitter-sensing neurons completely suppresses this response.
source: These results afford an explanation for the observation that fed flies normally fail to exhibit PER to acetic acid. Our data suggest that acetic acid activates sugar-sensing neurons, which promote an appetitive response, but in the fed state simultaneous activation of bitter-sensing neurons completely suppresses this response.
evidence: Inferred from genetic silencing experiments showing unmasking of appetitive response when bitter neurons are silenced.

claim: Silencing the bitter neurons eliminates suppression of the appetitive response to acetic acid, unmasking the appetitive response.
source: Silencing the bitter neurons eliminates this suppression, unmasking the appetitive response.
evidence: Inferred from genetic silencing experiments.

claim: Silencing the bitter neurons resulted in enhanced PER to acetic acid in starved flies.
source: Silencing the bitter neurons resulted not only in the emergence of PER to acetic acid in fed flies but also enhanced PER to acetic acid in starved flies (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PER to 10% acetic acid was observed in 70–80% of control flies and this value increased to 96% upon bitter neuron silencing.
source: PER to 10% acetic acid was observed in 70–80% of control flies and this value increased to 96% upon bitter neuron silencing (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Silencing bitter neurons in starved flies did not affect PER to sucrose.
source: Silencing bitter neurons in starved flies did not affect PER to sucrose (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Even in the starved state, bitter neurons suppress PER to acetic acid.
source: These results demonstrate that even in the starved state, bitter neurons suppress PER to acetic acid.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing enhanced PER when bitter neurons are silenced in starved flies.

claim: Bitter neuron silencing has a stronger effect on acetic acid-induced PER in fed flies than in starved flies.
source: The observation that bitter neuron silencing has a stronger effect on acetic acid-induced PER in fed flies (Figure 4B) than in starved flies (Figure 4C) suggests that activity within the bitter-sensing circuit is suppressed in the starved state.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experimental data in fed and starved flies.

claim: Activity within the bitter-sensing circuit is suppressed in the starved state.
source: The observation that bitter neuron silencing has a stronger effect on acetic acid-induced PER in fed flies (Figure 4B) than in starved flies (Figure 4C) suggests that activity within the bitter-sensing circuit is suppressed in the starved state.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experimental data in fed and starved flies.

claim: PER to sucrose is increased by starvation.
source: We and others observe that PER to sucrose is increased by starvation, indicating that the neural pathway for sugar-sensing is upregulated by hunger (Figure 1B; Inagaki et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to previous study.

claim: The neural pathway for sugar-sensing is upregulated by hunger.
source: We and others observe that PER to sucrose is increased by starvation, indicating that the neural pathway for sugar-sensing is upregulated by hunger (Figure 1B; Inagaki et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and citation to previous study.

claim: In control flies, starvation strongly increased PER to acetic acid: ~20% of fed flies and 70–80% of starved flies responded at the highest concentration.
source: In control flies, starvation strongly increased PER to acetic acid:~20% of fed flies and 70–80% of starved flies responded at the highest concentration (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Upon bitter neuron silencing the difference between PER in fed and starved flies was still observed, but was much smaller in magnitude: 68% of fed flies and 96% of starved flies responded at the highest concentration.
source: Upon bitter neuron silencing the difference between PER in fed and starved flies was still observed, but was much smaller in magnitude: 68% of fed flies and 96% of starved flies responded at the highest concentration (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The starvation-dependent enhancement of PER in bitter-silenced flies is likely to reflect the enhancement of the sugar-sensing circuit.
source: This starvation-dependent enhancement of PER in bitter-silenced flies is likely to reflect the enhancement of the sugar-sensing circuit.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing residual hunger effect after bitter neuron silencing.

claim: In fed flies, bitter neurons strongly suppress the appetitive response to acetic acid mediated by sugar neurons.
source: These results reveal a state-dependent interaction between the bitter- and sugar-sensing circuits that affords a logic for the behavioral switch. In fed flies, bitter neurons strongly suppress the appetitive response to acetic acid mediated by sugar neurons.
evidence: Inferred from genetic silencing experiments.

claim: Hunger results in a behavioral switch that increases PER both by suppressing the bitter-sensing circuit and enhancing the sugar-sensing circuit.
source: Hunger results in a behavioral switch that increases PER both by suppressing the bitter-sensing circuit and enhancing the sugar-sensing circuit.
evidence: Inferred from genetic silencing experiments comparing fed and starved flies.

claim: IR25a and IR76b function in tarsal sugar-sensing neurons to detect fatty acids.
source: Two members of the ionotropic receptor (IR) family of chemoreceptors, IR25a and IR76b, function in tarsal sugar-sensing neurons to detect fatty acids and in a separate population of tarsal sour-sensing neurons to detect organic and inorganic acids (Ahn et al., 2017; Chen and Amrein, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IR25a and IR76b function in a separate population of tarsal sour-sensing neurons to detect organic and inorganic acids.
source: Two members of the ionotropic receptor (IR) family of chemoreceptors, IR25a and IR76b, function in tarsal sugar-sensing neurons to detect fatty acids and in a separate population of tarsal sour-sensing neurons to detect organic and inorganic acids (Ahn et al., 2017; Chen and Amrein, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IR25a and IR76b mediate salt detection in multiple classes of labellar taste neurons, including sugar-sensing neurons.
source: These IRs also mediate salt detection in multiple classes of labellar taste neurons, including sugar-sensing neurons (Zhang et al., 2013; Jaeger et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Starved flies carrying mutations in Ir25a or Ir76b showed robust PER to 1–10% acetic acid.
source: Starved flies carrying mutations in Ir25a or Ir76b showed robust PER to 1–10% acetic acid, indicating that these receptors are not required for the appetitive response to acetic acid (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and D.

claim: IR25a and IR76b are not required for the appetitive response to acetic acid.
source: Starved flies carrying mutations in Ir25a or Ir76b showed robust PER to 1–10% acetic acid, indicating that these receptors are not required for the appetitive response to acetic acid (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and D).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing PER to acetic acid in mutant flies.

claim: Fed flies carrying IR25a or IR76b mutations showed very low levels of PER to acetic acid.
source: Fed flies carrying IR25a or IR76b mutations showed very low levels of PER to acetic acid, indicating that the aversive pathway that suppresses acetic acid-evoked PER in the fed state remains intact (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and E.

claim: The aversive pathway that suppresses acetic acid-evoked PER in the fed state remains intact in IR25a or IR76b mutants.
source: Fed flies carrying IR25a or IR76b mutations showed very low levels of PER to acetic acid, indicating that the aversive pathway that suppresses acetic acid-evoked PER in the fed state remains intact (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and E).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing low PER to acetic acid in fed mutant flies.

claim: IR25a and IR76b are not required for either appetitive or aversive responses to acetic acid.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that IR25a and IR76b are not required for either appetitive or aversive responses to acetic acid.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data with IR25a and IR76b mutants.

claim: Strong GCaMP responses to acetic acid were observed in sugar neurons in both fed and starved flies.
source: Strong GCaMP responses to acetic acid were observed in sugar neurons in both fed and starved flies, with the peak response to acetic acid about half of that observed with 500 mM sucrose (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: The peak response to acetic acid in sugar neurons was about half of that observed with 500 mM sucrose.
source: Strong GCaMP responses to acetic acid were observed in sugar neurons in both fed and starved flies, with the peak response to acetic acid about half of that observed with 500 mM sucrose (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Sugar neurons in 27 of 28 fed or starved flies responded to acetic acid at levels greater than the water response.
source: Despite this variability, sugar neurons in 27 of 28 fed or starved flies responded to acetic acid at levels greater than the water response.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Acetic acid activated bitter-sensing neurons with peak responses about 30% of those obtained with 1 mM lobeline.
source: Acetic acid activated the bitter neurons with peak responses about 30% of those obtained with 1 mM lobeline (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Neurons in the majority of both fed and starved flies responded to acetic acid (15/18 fed flies and 16/18 starved flies).
source: As in the sugar neurons, acetic acid responses in bitter neurons often appeared more variable across trials and flies than responses to bitter (Figure 5H; Figure 5—figure supplement 2), but neurons in the majority of both fed and starved flies responded to acetic acid (15/18 fed flies and 16/18 starved flies).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Only the S-b class of bitter neurons exhibited a significant peak response to acetic acid when compared to the response to water.
source: We imaged the acetic acid response of four different subclasses of bitter neurons (Weiss et al., 2011) and observed that only the S-b class exhibited a significant peak response when compared to the response to water (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Acetic acid activates both sugar- and bitter-sensing taste neurons.
source: Overall, these results show that acetic acid activates both sugar- and bitter-sensing taste neurons.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: In sugar neurons, dose-dependent responses were observed as the concentration was increased from 0.01% to 1%, but the response diminished slightly at 5%.
source: In sugar neurons, we observed dose-dependent responses as the concentration was increased from 0.01% to 1%, but the response diminished slightly at 5% (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Bitter neurons failed to show dose dependence in the concentration range of 0.01% to 5% acetic acid.
source: Bitter neurons failed to show dose dependence in this concentration range (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Bitter neurons fail to show clear dose-dependent responses to acetic acid.
source: Overall, we find that bitter neurons fail to show clear dose-dependent responses to acetic acid and sugar neurons show dose dependence only at low concentrations.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Sugar neurons show dose dependence only at low concentrations of acetic acid.
source: Overall, we find that bitter neurons fail to show clear dose-dependent responses to acetic acid and sugar neurons show dose dependence only at low concentrations.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Water-sensing neurons responded broadly to several taste stimuli at levels that were inversely related to their osmolarity.
source: Water-sensing neurons responded broadly to several taste stimuli at levels that were inversely related to their osmolarity (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: When the low-osmolarity response of water-sensing neurons was blocked by adding PEG to each taste solution, acetic acid did not activate the water-sensing neurons beyond the level elicited by PEG alone.
source: When the low-osmolarity response of water-sensing neurons was blocked by adding the high molecular mass polymer polyethylene glycol (PEG) to each taste solution, acetic acid did not activate the water-sensing neurons beyond the level elicited by PEG alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 6C–D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6C-D.

claim: Acetic acid activates water-sensing neurons solely by the osmolarity-sensing mechanism.
source: Acetic acid therefore activates water-sensing neurons solely by the osmolarity-sensing mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from calcium imaging data with PEG.

claim: The responses to acetic acid in sugar- and bitter-sensing neurons are specific and are likely to be mediated by receptors that recognize acetic acid.
source: Thus, the responses to acetic acid in sugar- and bitter-sensing neurons are specific and are likely to be mediated by receptors that recognize acetic acid.
evidence: Inferred from calcium imaging data showing specific responses in sugar and bitter neurons but not water neurons.

claim: Previous studies suggest that hunger increases sugar neuron responses to sucrose and suppresses bitter neuron responses to lobeline.
source: Previous studies suggest that hunger increases sugar neuron responses to sucrose and suppresses bitter neuron responses to lobeline (Inagaki et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014; LeDue et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A trend toward increased sucrose responses in sugar neurons after starvation was observed (p=0.063 for the effect of starvation, two-way ANOVA).
source: We observed a trend toward increased sucrose responses in sugar neurons after starvation (p=0.063 for the effect of starvation, two-way ANOVA), but lobeline responses of bitter neurons did not differ between fed and starved flies (Figure 5C–D and G–H).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C-D and G-H.

claim: Lobeline responses of bitter neurons did not differ between fed and starved flies.
source: We observed a trend toward increased sucrose responses in sugar neurons after starvation (p=0.063 for the effect of starvation, two-way ANOVA), but lobeline responses of bitter neurons did not differ between fed and starved flies (Figure 5C–D and G–H).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C-D and G-H.

claim: In both sugar and bitter neurons, starved flies showed significantly higher responses than fed flies to 1% but not 5% acetic acid.
source: We then examined sensory neuron responses to acetic acid in fed and starved flies. In both sugar and bitter neurons, starved flies showed significantly higher responses than fed flies to 1% but not 5% acetic acid (Figure 5C–D and G–H).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C-D and G-H.

claim: Hunger increased the average peak response to 1% acetic acid from 117% to 166% ∆F/F0 in sugar neurons.
source: Hunger increased the average peak response to 1% acetic acid from 117% to 166% ∆F/F0 in sugar neurons and from 46% to 87% ∆F/F0 in bitter neurons.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Hunger increased the average peak response to 1% acetic acid from 46% to 87% ∆F/F0 in bitter neurons.
source: Hunger increased the average peak response to 1% acetic acid from 117% to 166% ∆F/F0 in sugar neurons and from 46% to 87% ∆F/F0 in bitter neurons.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Sensory neuron modulation is not likely to account for the behavioral switch in the acetic acid response.
source: The striking effects of internal state on this behavior may therefore reflect state-dependent modulation of both the sugar and bitter circuits downstream of the sensory neurons.
evidence: Inferred from calcium imaging data showing enhancement of both sugar and bitter neuron responses, which does not match behavioral changes.

claim: The striking effects of internal state on acetic acid behavior may reflect state-dependent modulation of both the sugar and bitter circuits downstream of the sensory neurons.
source: The striking effects of internal state on this behavior may therefore reflect state-dependent modulation of both the sugar and bitter circuits downstream of the sensory neurons.
evidence: Inferred from calcium imaging data and behavioral data.

claim: Innate behaviors are mediated by neural circuits that are genetically determined.
source: Innate behaviors are observed in naive animals without prior learning or experience, suggesting that they are mediated by neural circuits that are genetically determined.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Innate behavioral responses can exhibit flexibility and can be modulated by experience, expectation, and internal state.
source: However, innate behavioral responses can also exhibit flexibility and can be modulated by experience, expectation, and internal state (Bargmann, 2012; Ding and Perkel, 2014; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Taste circuits in flies and mice appear to be anatomically and functionally programmed to elicit an innate appetitive or aversive response.
source: Taste circuits in flies and mice appear to be anatomically and functionally programmed to elicit an innate appetitive or aversive response, ensuring that animals consume nutritious foods and avoid the ingestion of toxins (Liman et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Acetic acid activates both the sugar and bitter pathways, which have opposing effects on feeding behavior.
source: Acetic acid activates both the sugar and bitter pathways, which have opposing effects on feeding behavior.
evidence: Supported by genetic silencing and calcium imaging data.

claim: The choice of behaviors in response to acetic acid is determined by internal state.
source: The choice of behaviors is determined by internal state: hunger shifts the response from aversion to attraction by enhancing the appetitive sugar pathway as well as suppressing the aversive bitter pathway (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by genetic silencing experiments and behavioral data.

claim: The activation of bitter neurons by organic acids has been observed previously by electrophysiologic recording of labellar sensilla.
source: The activation of bitter neurons by organic acids has been observed previously by electrophysiologic recording of labellar sensilla, and these acids result in taste aversion (Charlu et al., 2013; Rimal et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Organic acids result in taste aversion.
source: The activation of bitter neurons by organic acids has been observed previously by electrophysiologic recording of labellar sensilla, and these acids result in taste aversion (Charlu et al., 2013; Rimal et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A subset of bitter neurons serve as a pH sensor eliciting taste aversion.
source: The observation that bitter neurons respond not only to organic acids but also to hydrochloric acid suggested that a subset of bitter neurons serve as a pH sensor eliciting taste aversion (Charlu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Rimal et al. (2019) recently identified IR7a as a narrowly tuned acetic acid receptor acting in bitter neurons.
source: However, Rimal et al. (2019) recently identified IR7a as a narrowly tuned acetic acid receptor acting in bitter neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Two studies have reported that whereas acetic acid activates bitter neurons, it fails to activate sugar neurons.
source: Two studies have reported that whereas acetic acid activates bitter neurons, it fails to activate sugar neurons (Charlu et al., 2013; Rimal et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In previous studies, acetic acid activated S-type sensilla, which contain both bitter and sugar neurons, but failed to activate L-type sensilla, which contain sugar neurons but not bitter neurons.
source: In these studies acetic acid activated S-type sensilla, which contain both bitter and sugar neurons, but failed to activate L-type sensilla, which contain sugar neurons but not bitter neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mutants lacking IR7a, S-type sensilla continue to exhibit weak responses to acetic acid, which may represent responses of sugar neurons.
source: Rimal et al. (2019) observe that in mutants lacking IR7a, S-type sensilla continue to exhibit weak responses to acetic acid, which may represent responses of sugar neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The activation of different classes of sensory neurons by a single tastant has been observed for salt, the long chain fatty acid hexanoic acid, as well as for acetic acid.
source: The activation of different classes of sensory neurons by a single tastant has been observed for salt (Zhang et al., 2013; Jaeger et al., 2018), the long chain fatty acid, hexanoic acid (Ahn et al., 2017), as well as for acetic acid in this study.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and data from this study.

claim: In both flies and mammals, low salt concentrations elicit attraction whereas high salt results in aversion and these opposing behaviors are mediated by distinct classes of sensory neurons.
source: In both flies and mammals, low salt concentrations elicit attraction whereas high salt results in aversion and these opposing behaviors are mediated by distinct classes of sensory neurons (Zhang et al., 2013; Jaeger et al., 2018; Chandrashekar et al., 2010; Oka et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hexanoic acid, a caloric source, activates fatty acid receptors in sugar neurons and at high concentrations activates a different receptor in bitter neurons.
source: Hexanoic acid, a caloric source, activates fatty acid receptors in sugar neurons and at high concentrations activates a different receptor in bitter neurons (Ahn et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Hunger enhances olfactory attraction to cider vinegar, increases sugar sensitivity, and decreases bitter sensitivity.
source: Previous studies have observed that hunger enhances olfactory attraction to cider vinegar, increases sugar sensitivity, and decreases bitter sensitivity (Root et al., 2011; Inagaki et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hunger modulates behavioral responses to sugar and bitter at least in part by modulating the activity of the initial neurons in these pathways, the sensory neurons.
source: Previous studies suggest that hunger modulates behavioral responses to sugar and bitter at least in part by modulating the activity of the initial neurons in these pathways, the sensory neurons (Inagaki et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014; LeDue et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The response to sugar extends to multiple behaviors beyond PER including ingestion, swallowing, and suppression of locomotion, each of which is likely to be modulated by hunger.
source: The response to sugar extends to multiple behaviors beyond PER including ingestion, swallowing, and suppression of locomotion, each of which is likely to be modulated by hunger (Pool and Scott, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Modulation at the level of sensory neurons affords gain control that will result in changes in all behaviors elicited by gustatory neurons.
source: Modulation at the level of sensory neurons affords gain control that will result in changes in all behaviors elicited by gustatory neurons.
evidence: This is a logical inference about neural circuit function.

claim: Modulation of downstream taste neurons facilitating sensorimotor transformations could afford a flexibility enabling independent control of different behavioral programs driven by the same taste stimulus.
source: Modulation of downstream taste neurons facilitating sensorimotor transformations could afford a flexibility enabling independent control of different behavioral programs driven by the same taste stimulus.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.
